title: Quickstart
text:
The container needs the acquisition geometry, because every reconstruction here is calibrated — the fusion weights are functions of spatial frequency, so the code has to know what a pixel is worth.
import numpy as np
from scatterem import Dataset4dstem

array = np.load("my_4dstem.npy")   # (scan_y, scan_x, det_y, det_x)

dataset = Dataset4dstem.from_array(
    array,
    energy=300e3,                   # accelerating voltage, eV
    semiconvergence_angle=19.7e-3,  # convergence semi-angle, rad
    scan_step=0.25,                 # scan pitch, Angstrom
    device="cuda",
)
scan_step may be a scalar or a (dy, dx) pair. The reciprocal pixel size dk is measured from the bright-field disk rather than taken on faith — see Calibration, which is where most reconstruction problems actually live.

title: Quickstart
text:
Fit the aberrations
The reconstruction needs a decent aberration estimate, and the autofocus finds one by maximising image sharpness. It is a local optimisation, so it needs a starting point:
dataset.meta.aberrations.array[0] = -50.0   # defocus, Angstrom
dataset.determine_aberrations_(correct_order=2)






Give it a defocus



With meta.aberrations all zero the autofocus has nothing to descend from, and it raises rather than silently returning something arbitrary. Any estimate within a factor of two or so of the truth is enough; the sign matters more than the magnitude.
Index 0 is C10, and defocus == -C10.


correct_order=2 fits up to second order (defocus, two-fold astigmatism, coma, three-fold astigmatism). Raise it to reach spherical aberration; the higher orders need more signal to constrain.
The autofocus holds the scan rotation fixed, so meta.rotation must already be right on the way in. If you do not know it, see Calibration.

title: Quickstart
text:
Reconstruct
ptycho     = dataset.direct_ptychography()
dark_field = dataset.tilt_corrected_dark_field()
fused      = dataset.fused_full_field()
Each takes upsample, which defaults to "nyquist" — the factor that brings the output pitch to the resolution the data can actually support, rather than a round number someone picked. Pass a float to override.
All three cache on the dataset, so fused_full_field() reuses the two channel reconstructions if you already ran them with the same parameters.

title: Quickstart
text:
Look at the result
from scatterem.vis.reconstruction_sampling import reconstruction_sampling
from scatterem.vis.visualization import show_2d

fig, ax = show_2d(fused, sampling=reconstruction_sampling(dataset, fused))
fig.savefig("fused.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
Passing the sampling is what makes the scale bar read in Ångström instead of a.u. — and it must be the reconstruction’s sampling, not the dataset’s. The output is upsampled, so dataset.sampling would overstate the bar by the upsample factor: four-fold on the paper’s Fig. 4.

Save and reload
dataset.save("carbon.h5")
same = Dataset4dstem.load("carbon.h5", device="cuda")
The file records which fields it contains. If you later add or rename a field on the class, loading an old file fails and names the difference, rather than handing you a half-populated object. See scatterem.io.store.

Python 3.10 or newer. Ten runtime dependencies, all from PyPI.

title: Install
text:
About the GPU
A CUDA GPU is not optional in practice. The reconstructions are FFT- and kernel-bound, and the NVIDIA Warp kernels that do the direct-ptychography work need one for anything past a small test. Everything runs on CPU, just slowly enough that you would not want to.
If the default torch wheel does not match your driver, install torch first from the index that does, then install this package — pip will leave your existing torch alone:
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
pip install git+https://github.com/scatterem/scatterem
import scatterem initialises Warp, which compiles a few kernels the first time and prints a short banner. That is expected, and it is cached afterwards.






Two side effects on import



import scatterem sets torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("medium") (TF32) and calls warp.init(). Both are inherited from the library the published reconstructions ran under, so results match — but if your own code depends on matmul precision, set it again after importing.

title: Install
text:
For STEM-EELS simulation
The simulation code needs nothing beyond the above to run, but it needs gpaw to be quantitative: it supplies the all-electron bound and continuum radial wavefunctions the ionization transition potentials are built from.
pip install gpaw gpaw-data
Prebuilt wheels are available, so this does not normally need libxc, MPI or a Fortran toolchain. Without it the code falls back to hydrogenic orbitals and a free continuum, which exercise the whole pipeline but do not give accurate cross-sections — see Simulate STEM-EELS.
Atomic wavefunctions and transition potentials are cached on disk once computed. Set SCATTEREM_EELS_CACHE to put that somewhere with room.

title: Simulate STEM-EELS
text:
This is the forward problem: given a structure, produce the core-loss EELS signal a STEM would record. There is no EELS reconstruction here.
Three algorithms compute the same physics at very different cost, and the one you want depends on what you want out:
The cube keeps the whole diffraction pattern at every scan position, so it is the general output and the expensive one. The map integrates over an EELS collection aperture. The same two-matrix path can also retain individual detector beams for qEELS and PACBED — see BiP-PRISM. If an elemental map is what you are after, do not simulate a cube and sum it.

title: Simulate STEM-EELS
text:
A structure
Structure is a plain NumPy container: orthorhombic cell edges in Ångström, and an (n, 4) table of fractional coordinates with atomic numbers.
import numpy as np
from scatterem.simulation import Structure

a = 3.905
sto = Structure(
    np.array([a, a, a]),
    np.array([                  # [x, y, z, Z], fractional coordinates
        [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 38],    # Sr
        [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 22],    # Ti
        [0.5, 0.5, 0.0, 8],     # O
        [0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 8],
        [0.0, 0.5, 0.5, 8],
    ]),
    dwf=None,                   # <u^2> per atom; None gives every atom 0.01 A^2
).tile(x=4, y=4, z=8)           # 15.6 x 15.6 x 31.2 A, 640 atoms
Structure.fromfile reads the three formats the simulation community uses — Prismatic .xyz, VESTA .p1 and .xtl. A non-orthorhombic cell is converted to an orthorhombic supercell at construction, because that is the only cell the multislice understands.






dwf is \(\langle u^2 \rangle\), one-dimensional



Column 5 of Structure.atoms holds the one-dimensional mean-square thermal displacement in Å², not the Debye-Waller \(B\) and not the three-dimensional total. \(B = 8\pi^2 \langle u^2 \rangle\). Getting the convention wrong makes the frozen-phonon smearing wrong by \(\sqrt{3}\).

title: Simulate STEM-EELS
text:
A cube
from scatterem.simulation import StemEelsSimulator

sim = StemEelsSimulator(
    sto,
    eV=100e3,                    # probe energy
    semiconvergence_angle=25.0,  # mrad
    pixels=(128, 128),           # real-space grid across the cell
    scan=(16, 16),               # scan positions
    edge=(22, 2, 1),             # Ti L: (Z, n, l) of the ionized subshell
    epsilon=10.0,                # eV above the ionization threshold
    num_slices=16,
    prism=True,
    interpolation_factor=2,
    device="cuda",
)

result = sim.simulate()
result.cube          # (16, 16, 128, 128), real, non-negative
result.sampling      # detector (dky, dkx) in 1/A
result.energy_losses # the per-transition losses summed into the cube, eV
edge names the bound orbital that is ionized, as (Z, n, l): Ti L is (22, 2, 1), O K is (8, 1, 0), Fe L is (26, 2, 1). Every atom of that Z in the structure ionizes; there is no site selection.
epsilon is the energy of the ejected electron above the threshold, so it picks a point along the edge rather than an absolute energy loss. The onset is the binding energy, and the code reports the resulting loss in result.energy_losses.






semiconvergence_angle is in milliradians here



Dataset4dstem.from_array on the reconstruction side takes radians; the simulator takes mrad. The same is true of detector_mrad below. A factor of 1000 produces a probe that is either the whole grid or a single pixel, so the failure is loud — but it costs a run.


The diffraction patterns are corner-origin, like everything else in reciprocal space here. torch.fft.fftshift before plotting.

title: Simulate STEM-EELS
section: An energy window, and several edges
text:
An energy window, and several edges
A single epsilon is one point on the edge. To integrate a real energy-filtered window, sweep it:
result = sim.simulate_window((5.0, 45.0), n_energies=8)
result.energy_range   # (onset + 5, onset + 45) eV
The continuum states are energy-normalised, so trapezoid-integrating over epsilon is the signal collected in that loss window. eps_min must be greater than zero — the energy-normalised continuum diverges at threshold.
Several edges in one pass is much cheaper than several simulators, because the elastic transmission functions are the dynamical scattering of the whole structure and do not care which element ionizes:
results = sim.simulate_edges([(22, 2, 1), (8, 1, 0)], energy_range=(5.0, 45.0))
ti, o = results[(22, 2, 1)], results[(8, 1, 0)]
Transmissions and probes are shared across every edge and every frozen phonon; only the transition potentials are rebuilt. The cost is memory — all the edges’ transition-potential stacks are resident at once so that one frozen-phonon sweep can serve them all.

title: Simulate STEM-EELS
section: Transition potentials, and the GPAW question
text:
Transition potentials, and the GPAW question
The ionization operator \(H_{n0}\) is built from atomic radial wavefunctions, and where those come from decides whether your numbers mean anything.
from scatterem.simulation import gpaw_available
gpaw_available()
With gpaw installed (backend="auto" finds it) bound states come from an all-electron atomic DFT calculation and continuum states from Numerov integration of the radial Schrödinger equation in that all-electron potential. This is the physically accurate path.
Without it the code falls back to a hydrogenic bound state and a free spherical-Bessel continuum. That runs the entire pipeline and is what the test suite uses, but it is not quantitatively accurate — the selection rules and the shape of the pipeline are right, the cross-sections are not.
pip install "scatterem[eels] @ git+https://github.com/scatterem/scatterem.git@v0.3" gpaw-data






backend="auto" will silently give you hydrogenic orbitals



If GPAW is not importable, "auto" falls back rather than raising. Check gpaw_available() before a production run, or pass backend="gpaw" to make a missing install an error instead of a quiet loss of accuracy.


Computed wavefunctions and potentials are cached on disk, keyed by their physical parameters, so a re-run does not redo the atomic calculations. Point the cache somewhere with room via SCATTEREM_EELS_CACHE.
Two parameters worth knowing: order sets how many angular-momentum channels are summed (default 1 keeps the monopole and both dipole channels, which is what the published treatments use), and potential_scale is an empirical multiplier on the GPAW continuum potential — 1.0 is the Brown 2019 physics, abTEM uses 1.02, and it mostly moves the \(l' = l\) monopole s-wave.

title: Simulate STEM-EELS
text:
A full-resolution elemental map
The map is the BiP-PRISM path, and it is a lower-level call: it takes the probe aperture, the transmission functions, the transition potentials and the scan directly, rather than being driven from StemEelsSimulator.
import numpy as np
import torch
from scatterem.simulation import (
    build_transition_potentials,
    make_transmission_functions,
    subshell_transitions,
)
from scatterem.simulation.eels import prism_eels_image
from scatterem.utils.physics import electron_wavelength

eV, pixels, num_slices, device = 100e3, (128, 128), 16, "cuda"
wavelength = electron_wavelength(eV)
gridsize = (float(sto.unitcell[0]), float(sto.unitcell[1]))
sampling = (gridsize[0] / pixels[0], gridsize[1] / pixels[1])

transmissions = make_transmission_functions(
    sto, pixels, eV,
    subslices=[(i + 1) / num_slices for i in range(num_slices)],
    displacements=False, fftout=False, device=device,
).to(torch.complex64)

tp = build_transition_potentials(
    subshell_transitions(22, 2, 1, 10.0),   # Ti L at 10 eV above threshold
    22, pixels, sampling, eV, device=device,
)

# Probe-forming aperture, normalised to unit real-space intensity.
qy = np.fft.fftfreq(pixels[0], d=sampling[0])
qx = np.fft.fftfreq(pixels[1], d=sampling[1])
q2 = qy[:, None] ** 2 + qx[None, :] ** 2
probe_q = torch.as_tensor(
    (q2 <= (25e-3 / wavelength) ** 2).astype(np.complex64), device=device
)
probe_q = probe_q / (probe_q.abs().pow(2).sum() / probe_q.numel()).sqrt()

# Scan grid in pixels, and the sites that ionize.
scan_shape = (32, 32)
sy = (np.arange(scan_shape[0]) + 0.5) * pixels[0] / scan_shape[0]
sx = (np.arange(scan_shape[1]) + 0.5) * pixels[1] / scan_shape[1]
scan_pixels = torch.as_tensor(
    np.stack(np.meshgrid(sy, sx, indexing="ij"), -1).reshape(-1, 2), device=device
)
sites = sto.atoms[np.round(sto.atoms[:, 3]).astype(int) == 22, :3]

ti_map = prism_eels_image(
    probe_q, transmissions, tp, sites, scan_pixels,
    wavelength=wavelength,
    gridsize=gridsize,
    slice_distance=float(sto.unitcell[2]) / num_slices,
    detector_mrad=25.0,               # EELS collection semi-angle
    interpolation_factor=2,
    inelastic_crop=4,
    scan_shape=scan_shape,
    partition=dict(n_radial=4),       # partition S1
    partition_s2=dict(n_radial=4),    # ... and S2 -- this is the "Bi" in BiP
)
Dropping both partition arguments gives the exact dual matrix, which is the oracle to check against on a small cell — and the thing that does not fit on one GPU at full resolution.






There is no simulate_map convenience method yet



StemEelsSimulator drives the cube paths only. The map is assembled from the public building blocks above, as shown. If you find yourself writing this more than once, wrap it.

title: Simulate STEM-EELS
text:
Momentum-resolved output and PACBED
Use the same inputs as the elemental-map call above. With qeels_axis="both", the result is (patterns, q_pixels): patterns has shape scan_shape + (n_detector_beams,) (or (P, n_detector_beams) without scan_shape), and q_pixels has shape (n_detector_beams, 2) in (qy, qx) order. Divide each coordinate column by its corresponding gridsize to obtain inverse Ångström. Average patterns over the scan dimensions for PACBED.
qeels_axis=0 or 1 returns a one-axis momentum projection and a sorted one-dimensional coordinate array. Summing the last axis of any resolved output recovers the integrated map from the same settings. Prefer interpolation_factor=1 when retaining detector coordinates; a larger factor subsamples the detector.
The v0.3 defaults are mag_preserve=True, focal_backprop=None, and contract="columns". Detector vacuum-phase removal is enabled when the detector is partitioned. See accuracy and focal referencing for their meaning and convergence checks.

title: Simulate STEM-EELS
section: What it costs, and the levers
text:
What it costs, and the levers
Four knobs, in rough order of how much they buy:
partition / partition_s2 (dict(n_radial=N)) build each scattering matrix on a sparse set of parent beams instead of every beam. This is the memory lever, and on a large map it is worth an order of magnitude or more — but only once the matrices are what is filling the card. On a small problem it saves nothing and costs a little time. It is also approximate, and the detector side is the demanding one: see accuracy.
interpolation_factor (\(f\)) subsamples the aperture beams by \(f^2\). The condition for it to be valid is that the probe must fit inside a \(1/f\) fraction of the cell around the atom; violate it and neighbouring periodic copies of the probe leak in. For the 4D-STEM cube it is the only lever on the exit leg, since partitioning there touches \(\mathcal{S}_1\) alone. Mind the scale it carries — see below.
inelastic_crop restricts the per-atom contraction to a (Ny, Nx) // inelastic_crop window. \(H_{n0}\) has sub-ångström support, so a generous crop costs nothing in accuracy and saves the contraction’s largest intermediate. None uses the full grid and is exact.
num_frozen_phonons with displacements=True averages over thermal configurations. Cost is strictly linear in the count; one configuration is enough for a smoke test and wrong for anything quantitative.
Two things that are not levers: the number of scan positions barely moves the PRISM and BiP-PRISM cost, which is the entire point of the scattering matrix, and raising the detector angle raises \(n_{\text{det}}\) and therefore the \(\mathcal{S}_2\) build.

title: Simulate STEM-EELS
text:
Checking your setup
The approximations compose, so check them one at a time on a cell small enough that the exact answer is affordable:
common = dict(
    eV=100e3, semiconvergence_angle=25.0, pixels=(128, 128), scan=(8, 8),
    edge=(22, 2, 1), epsilon=10.0, num_slices=16, device="cuda",
)

exact = StemEelsSimulator(sto, prism=False, **common).simulate().cube
prism = StemEelsSimulator(sto, prism=True, interpolation_factor=1, **common).simulate().cube

rel = float((prism - exact).norm() / exact.norm())
At \(f = 1\) PRISM reproduces the conventional multislice to rounding. On the SrTiO₃ cell above — 4×4×8 cells, 128², Ti L — that is rel-L2 \(10^{-4}\) and a correlation of 1.000000, and a large residual there means something is wrong with the setup rather than with the method.






interpolation_factor changes the absolute scale of the cube



Raising \(f\) preserves the pattern but multiplies the cube’s intensity by roughly \(f^2\). Measured on that same cell against the conventional result:

title: BiP-PRISM
text:
A core-loss STEM-EELS simulation is a double-channelling problem. The probe has to be propagated dynamically to an atom that ionizes, the ionization event has to be applied there, and the inelastically scattered wave has to be propagated dynamically from that atom to the detector. Both legs are multislice.
Written out, the conventional transition-potential multislice does this for every combination of scan position, ionized atom and transition channel. With \(P\) scan positions, \(N_a\) atoms of the ionized element and \(N_t\) channels, that is \(P N_a N_t\) exit-wave propagations. The scan is the painful factor: it is the one that grows when you ask for the atomic-resolution map you actually wanted.

With \(P\) scan positions, \(N_a\) atoms of the ionized element and \(N_t\) channels, that is \(P N_a N_t\) exit-wave propagations. The scan is the painful factor: it is the one that grows when you ask for the atomic-resolution map you actually wanted.

title: BiP-PRISM
section: The scattering matrix removes the scan
text:
The scattering matrix removes the scan
PRISM’s idea is that the entrance leg does not depend on where the probe is. A converged probe is a sum of plane waves over the aperture, and multislice is linear, so propagating each of the \(B\) aperture beams once gives a basis \(\mathcal{S}_1\) from which the probe at any scan position is recovered as a linear combination — the coefficients are the aperture’s phase ramps. One propagation of \(B\) columns replaces \(P\) propagations of one probe.
The exit leg yields to the same argument, and this is the step that makes detector-integrated maps cheap. Everything after the transition potential is linear too, so
\[
\psi_{\text{exit}}(\boldsymbol{\rho}) \;=\;
\mathcal{S}_2\Big[\,H_{n0}\sum_b c_b(\boldsymbol{\rho})\,\mathcal{S}_{1,b}\Big]
\;=\;
\sum_b c_b(\boldsymbol{\rho})\;\mathcal{S}_2\big[\,H_{n0}\,\mathcal{S}_{1,b}\big] .
\]
The expensive operator acts on the \(B\) columns, not on the \(P\) probes, and the scan is synthesised afterwards by the same coefficients that formed it. For a detector-integrated map \(\mathcal{S}_2\) can be built once per slice as a transpose multislice of the detector-accepted output beams — by reciprocity, running the detector backwards is the same calculation as running the source forwards — and then reused across every atom in that slice. The per-scan exit propagation disappears entirely. This is the dual-matrix algorithm of Brown, Ciston & Ophus.

title: BiP-PRISM
text:
What is left is memory
Having traded time for structure, the cost reappears as storage. \(\mathcal{S}_1\) is \(B\) complex arrays on the full \(N \times N\) grid; \(\mathcal{S}_2\) is \(n_{\text{det}}\) of them, and the detector is usually the wider aperture of the two. Both are resident. On the FePt nanoparticle below, the exact dual matrix needs 63 GB — more than any consumer card, and more than most cluster cards.

title: BiP-PRISM
text:
Partitioning both matrices
Beam partitioning attacks exactly this. Neighbouring beams in the aperture differ only by a small tilt, so their columns, once de-tilted, are locally similar. Build the matrix on a sparse set of \(B_p \ll B\) parent beams, and reconstruct the column you need for any beam by natural-neighbour interpolation of the parents — de-tilt, combine with the interpolation weights, re-tilt.
The reconstruction is only ever needed locally, and that is the point. The ionization operator \(H_{n0}(\mathbf{r} - \boldsymbol{\tau})\) has sub-ångström support around the atom at \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\), so it is the crop: the columns only have to be right inside a small window, never across the whole grid.
BiP-PRISM — bi-partitioned PRISM — applies this to both matrices at once: \(\mathcal{S}_1\) on parent aperture beams, \(\mathcal{S}_2\) on parent detector beams, each reconstructed on the crop window around the ionized atom immediately before the contraction
\[
\big[\mathcal{S}H_{n0}\big]_{db}
\;=\;
\sum_{\mathbf{r}\,\in\,\Omega_\tau}
\mathcal{S}_{2,d}(\mathbf{r})\,H_{n0}(\mathbf{r}-\boldsymbol{\tau})\,\mathcal{S}_{1,b}(\mathbf{r}) .
\]
Both reconstructions resolve before the contraction, on the window, and the window is small — so the resident matrices shrink from \(B\) and \(n_{\text{det}}\) columns to \(B_p\) each, while the arithmetic that consumes them is unchanged.






Resolved detector output



prism_transition_potential retains the full exit diffraction pattern with ordinary multislice on the exit leg, so its partition option applies to \(\mathcal{S}_1\) alone. prism_eels_image reconstructs both matrices and can also retain detector coordinates: use qeels_axis=0 or 1 for a momentum projection, or qeels_axis="both" for individual detector beams. Averaging these resolved patterns over probe positions gives core-loss-filtered PACBED. Summing the retained detector intensities recovers the elemental map.

title: BiP-PRISM
section: Accuracy, and the one caveat worth knowing
text:
Accuracy, and the one caveat worth knowing
Partitioning approximates the scattering columns on the inelastic crop window. For a double-partitioned calculation, both the probe and detector reconstruction errors matter. Increase partition and partition_s2 parent counts independently and compare with an unpartitioned calculation at the same grid, PRISM factor, energy window and detector aperture. This isolates partitioning error; convergence of the grid, slice thickness and crop is a separate check.
Version 0.3 corrects the detector reconstruction’s carrier signs. Detector columns start from conjugate plane waves, so their de-tilt and re-tilt signs are opposite to those of probe columns. It also removes each parent’s known quadratic vacuum propagation phase before interpolation and restores the target beam’s phase afterwards. These scalar factors work directly on the crop window. With all beams selected as parents, reconstruction recovers the unpartitioned columns; in vacuum, the corrected detector interpolation is exact even with sparse parents, up to floating-point error.
mag_preserve=True additionally uses the interpolated magnitudes and the phase of the complex natural-neighbour sum on crop windows. This is a heuristic for limiting amplitude loss, not a guarantee of absolute cross-section accuracy. Set mag_preserve=False for plain complex interpolation. For a detector-phase ablation, partition_s2=dict(n_radial=4, dechirp=False) keeps the corrected carrier signs but disables scalar vacuum-phase removal.

title: BiP-PRISM
text:
Focal referencing
focal_backprop=None is the default: interpolate at the current ionization plane. This differs from zero incident-probe defocus, which sets the probe’s entrance phase. Optional focal_backprop="centroid" references the probe parents by half the traversed depth, rounded to a slice, then propagates the interpolated columns forward to the ionization plane. A numeric value specifies the fraction of the traversed depth. Windowed forward propagation uses padding; its truncation must be converged separately. When every beam is a parent, the reference-plane round trip is skipped to preserve the exact cropped columns. No reference plane is assumed to minimize interpolation error universally.
The corrected large-map examples use zero incident defocus with focal back-propagation disabled. The single-column regime survey uses the explicit centroid setting. Scalar detector dechirping is independent of this spatial reference-plane operation.

title: BiP-PRISM
text:
Memory and runtime
Partitioning reduces resident scattering-matrix storage by replacing full beam sets with parent sets. The per-atom coupling and scan synthesis still cost time; reconstruction overhead can outweigh build savings on small problems. Measure both runtime and peak memory for the specimen and output mode of interest.
contract="columns" forms the beam-to-beam coupling before scan synthesis; contract="probe" forms the local probe first. Both compute the same observable within floating-point precision. scan_chunk bounds the number of scan positions processed together in the resolved-output and probe-contraction paths; it does not change the output definition.

title: scatterem
text:
A 4D-STEM dataset holds more information than any single reconstruction recovers. Direct ptychography reads the phase gradient encoded in the bright-field disk and recovers low and mid spatial frequencies with high efficiency, but its transfer falls away past the disk. Tilt-corrected dark field reads the parallax shift of scattering outside the disk and recovers high frequencies, but carries almost nothing at low ones. Neither channel spans the band on its own, and used alone each leaves a gap where the other is strong.
Fused full-field STEM combines them as an SSNR-weighted Wiener fusion, so each spatial frequency is taken from whichever channel measures it better. The result is one image with no missing band.
Run it now on a free GPU: the notebook installs the package, fetches one dataset from Zenodo and reconstructs it, with nothing to set up locally.
That is the whole pipeline. Each channel is also available on its own — dataset.direct_ptychography() and dataset.tilt_corrected_dark_field() — and all three share one calibration, so they land on the same grid.

Tilt-corrected dark-field reconstruction.
shift_method selects how each azimuthal dark-field segment is sub-pixel shifted (by its parallax shift) and accumulated onto the up-sampled grid:

"drizzle" (default) — area-overlap drizzle (box splat + hit-map normalization). Non-negative and ringing-free, which is the physically correct behaviour for counting data: at low dose the segment images are single electron counts and Fourier shifting turns each into a sinc with ~20% negative side-lobes. drizzle_pixfrac sets the drop size (fraction of an input pixel; 1.0 fills the grid from one frame) and drizzle_kde_sigma optionally Nadaraya-Watson-smooths sparse holes.
"fourier" — Fourier zero-pad upsample + phase-ramp shift. Marginally sharper on dense, well-sampled (high-dose) data, but rings on sparse data.

_segment_geometry is a private hook for callers that hold the aberrations ORTHOGONAL to everything else and sweep them (the depth section): pass the :class:_SegmentGeometry from :func:_tcdf_segment_geometry to skip rebuilding the masks and re-gathering the 4D array on every step.

simulate_window
simulate_window(self, energy_range: 'Tuple[float, float]', n_energies: 'int' = 16, batch_size: 'Optional[int]' = None) -> 'StemEelsResult'
Energy-integrated 4D-STEM-EELS over an energy-loss window.
Sweeps the continuum-electron energy epsilon across energy_range (energies above the ionization threshold, eV) on a uniform grid of n_energies points and trapezoid-integrates the per-energy datacubes.
Because the continuum states are energy-normalised (per unit energy), ∫ I(epsilon) d(epsilon) is the signal collected in the corresponding energy-loss window [onset + eps_min, onset + eps_max], where the edge onset = -E_bound is the binding energy of the ionized subshell. The mapping ΔE = epsilon + onset is linear, so integrating over epsilon equals integrating over energy loss.

title: API reference
text:
Parameters
energy_range : (float, float) (eps_min, eps_max) above threshold [eV]; eps_min must be > 0 (the energy-normalised continuum diverges at threshold) and eps_max > eps_min. n_energies : int Number of energies sampled across the window (>= 2). More points reduce the trapezoid-integration error at proportional cost. batch_size : int, optional Forwarded to the conventional multislice scan-position batching.

title: API reference
text:
Notes
Transition potentials are built once per energy (the GPAW continuum is additionally cached on disk), and the transmission functions are computed once per frozen phonon and reused across all energies. Memory scales with n_energies (one transition-potential stack is held per sampled energy).

simulate_edges
simulate_edges(self, edges: 'Sequence[Tuple[int, int, int]]', energy_range: 'Optional[Tuple[float, float]]' = None, n_energies: 'int' = 16, batch_size: 'Optional[int]' = None) -> "'dict[Tuple[int, int, int], StemEelsResult]'"
Simulate several ionization edges (elements/subshells) in one pass.
The elastic transmission functions and probes are shared across all edges – they are the dynamical scattering of the whole structure and do not depend on which element is ionized – so this is much cheaper than constructing a separate :class:StemEelsSimulator per element (which would recompute the transmissions, and the frozen-phonon passes, every time).

Build the x by y by z supercell IN PLACE.
The cell edge along dimension :math:d becomes :math:n_d times longer and every atom is replicated at all integer lattice translations, with the coordinates re-expressed as fractions of the NEW cell:
.. math::
f^{new}_d(, m) = , m_d < n_d .
Output ORDERING is part of the contract: copies are enumerated in C order over :math:m = (m_x, m_y, m_z) – flat index :math:m_x n_y n_z + m_y n_z + m_z – and the original atom order is preserved within each copy. The table is therefore copy-major and atom-minor: rows [c*n_atoms, (c+1)*n_atoms) belong to copy c. Consumers that pair a per-atom weight vector with structure.atoms rely on this.
Columns 3-5 (Z, occ, <u^2>) are copied verbatim into every replica; neither Title nor fractional_occupancy changes.

title: API reference
text:
Pipeline

Cartesian positions and the pivot: :math:r = f \odot L, :math:o = \mathrm{origin} \odot L, with :math:L the cell edge lengths.
:math:r' = (r - o) R + o with :math:R from :func:_rot_matrix.
.. warning::
Sign convention. R is the ACTIVE rotation of a COLUMN vector, but it is applied to ROW vectors on the right. Since r @ R = (R^T r^T)^T and :math:R^{\mathsf T} = R(-\theta), the atoms are rotated by minus theta about axis. Example: an atom at fractional (0.75, 0.5, 0.5) of a 4x4x4 A cell sits 1 A from the centre along +x, and rotate(pi/2, [0, 0, 1]) puts it at Cartesian (2, 1, 2), i.e. 1 A along -y. Using the textbook active convention here would mirror every tilt series.
Re-boxing, selected by (rebox, wrap):

rebox=False – keep the cell verbatim and just divide by it. Atoms leaving the box are neither wrapped nor clipped; a warning naming the observed fractional range is issued instead. Use this for a tilt SERIES of a vacuum-padded finite object, so that every tilt shares one cell, field of view and object placement.
rebox=True, wrap=True (default) – fit a new axis-aligned box to the rotated CELL CORNERS, using the five fractional corners 000, 100, 010, 001, 111: the new origin is their componentwise minimum and the new edge lengths their componentwise peak-to-peak range. Atoms are then mapped into that box modulo 1. Five corners are exact for a rotation about a cardinal axis (the remaining corners 110, 101, 011 add nothing to the bounding box there); for a general off-axis direction the box can be undersized, and the modulo-1 reduction then maps atoms into wrong periodic images.
rebox=True, wrap=False – fit the box to the true rotated ATOM extent: origin = componentwise minimum minus margin, edges = peak-to-peak plus 2*margin, with NO modulo-1 reduction. Exact for a finite, non-periodic specimen at an arbitrary tilt.

prism_transition_potential
prism_transition_potential(probe_q: 'Tensor', transmissions: 'Tensor', transition_potentials: 'TransitionPotentials', sites: 'np.ndarray', scan_pixels: 'Tensor', *, wavelength: 'float', gridsize: 'Sequence[float]', slice_distance: 'float', return_real_space: 'bool' = False, interpolation_factor=1, partition=None, scan_chunk: 'int' = 64) -> 'Tensor'
Dual-scattering-matrix PRISM STEM-EELS (Brown & Ophus).
Implements the two-scattering-matrix algorithm of Brown, Ciston & Ophus, Phys. Rev. Research 1, 033186 (2019), Eq. (11):
S_{n,iz} = S2 . F . H_{n0} . F^{-1} . S1,
where :math:\mathcal S_1 propagates the probe-forming plane waves from the entrance surface to the ionization slice iz and :math:\mathcal S_2 propagates the inelastically-scattered wave from iz to the exit surface.
The key to the full PRISM benefit (vs. :func:prism_transition_potential_hybrid) is the order of operations. Because every operator after :math:\mathcal S_1 is linear, the exit wave for scan position p is::
psi_exit(p) = S2[ H_n0 . (sum_b coeff_p[b] S1_col[b]) ]
            = sum_b coeff_p[b] * S2[ H_n0 . S1_col[b] ],
so the transition is applied to the Nbeams columns of :math:\mathcal S_1 and those columns are propagated to the exit (the action of :math:\mathcal S_2), then the scan positions are synthesised by the same linear combination used to form the probe. The expensive exit-surface multislice therefore runs Nbeams times per (site, transition) – independent of the number of scan positions P – instead of P times. For P >> Nbeams (a dense scan through a small aperture, the PRISM regime) this is the source of the near-linear scaling.
With the exact per-pixel scattering matrix (partition=None) the result is identical (to float rounding) to :func:prism_transition_potential_hybrid; this routine just reorders the work. Energy-filtered 4D output is preserved – S2 is applied as on-the-fly multislice of the column basis (the full exit diffraction pattern is kept, so no detector reduction is made). Detector-integrating the returned cube over an EELS aperture reproduces the Brown & Ophus I(x, y) image.
Shrinking the column count (two compatible levers).

interpolation_factor = f subsamples the aperture beams to Nbeams / f**2 columns – exact within the PRISM aliasing window – shrinking the exact columns of both legs (S1 build and exit) by f**2.
partition (e.g. {"n_radial": 4}) builds S1 on Bp << Nbeams parent beams (Pelz/Ophus partitioned PRISM), then reconstructs the exact aperture columns from the parents at the ionization plane and runs the same dual-S exit. This cheapens the S1 build + memory (Bp parent propagations) and is approximate (natural-neighbor reconstruction error – accurate in-focus / thin / small-aperture, degrading with thickness/aperture); the exit leg still propagates the reconstructed Nbeams / f**2 columns, so the dual-S P-independence is preserved. Note partitioning does not reduce the (usually dominant) exit leg – only the S1 build; interpolation_factor is the lever for the exit. The two compose (partition partitions the already-subsampled aperture). Unlike partitioning S2, this is correct: the reconstruction resolves the position-dependent NNW basis before H_{n0} is applied (see :meth:PartitionedScatteringMatrix.reconstruct_columns).

title: API reference
text:
Parameters
probe_q : Tensor (Ny, Nx) Probe-forming aperture in reciprocal space (complex). transmissions : Tensor (NZ, Ny, Nx) Elastic transmission functions (|T| = 1; no absorption). transition_potentials : TransitionPotentials Transition potentials (.array (n_trans, Ny, Nx), centred at origin). sites : ndarray (Nsite, 3) Fractional (y, x, z) of the ionized atoms. scan_pixels : Tensor (P, 2) Scan positions in pixels. wavelength, gridsize, slice_distance As elsewhere. detector_mrad : float EELS detector collection semi-angle [mrad]; output beams within it. interpolation_factor : int or (int, int) PRISM interpolation factor for S1 (and the scan crop region). inelastic_crop : int, optional Crop the transition-potential / scattering-matrix window to (Ny, Nx) // inelastic_crop around each atom (the localized transition). None uses the full grid (exact; equals the detector-integrated 4D dual-S). prism_mask : bool Restrict each atom’s contribution to scan positions within the PRISM 1/f crop region around it (matches the interpolation-factor periodicity). scan_shape : (int, int), optional If given, the flat (P,) image is reshaped to scan_shape. partition : dict, optional If given (e.g. {"n_radial": 4}), build S1 on Bp parent beams (:class:PartitionedScatteringMatrix) and reconstruct the exact aperture columns on each atom’s crop window via natural-neighbor interpolation. This cheapens the S1 build/advance + memory (Bp parents) at the cost of the NNW reconstruction error. None uses the exact per-pixel S1. Overlapping windows may reuse a full-grid reconstruction for one slice. This uses a conservative additional-workspace budget of 2 GiB shared with S2; sparse windows and active focal referencing retain windowed reconstruction. This budget is not a bound on total simulation memory. partition_s2 : dict, optional Same idea for S2 (the detector matrix): build the transpose multislice on Bp parent detector beams and NNW-reconstruct the detector columns on the crop window. Reduces the (often dominant) resident S2 storage from ndet to Bp columns; stacks a second NNW error on the detector side. None keeps the full per-beam S2. qeels_axis : {0, 1, “both”}, optional Momentum-resolved (qEELS) output. None (default) returns the scalar elemental map. 0 or 1 resolves that detector-momentum axis and projects (sums) the perpendicular one away: the per-detector-beam intensities |amp_d|^2 are binned by their signed frequency along qeels_axis instead of summed over all d. Summing the spectrum back over the resolved axis recovers the map exactly. Works with partition / partition_s2 (binning is post-|amp|^2); for a faithful resolved axis use interpolation_factor = 1 along it. "both" retains each detector beam separately (no projection). mag_preserve : bool, default True Magnitude-preserving NNW reconstruction of the partitioned columns: keep the complex-sum phase but restore the interpolated magnitude. Counters the phase- decoherence amplitude loss of the naive complex average (which underestimates the absolute scale ~2x at low parent count); converges to the exact result at full parents. Set False for the original (eq-14-style) behaviour. focal_backprop : float or “centroid”, optional Interpolate S1 parents at a Fresnel-referenced plane, then propagate the reconstructed window back. “centroid” uses half the traversed distance; a number specifies a fraction. A partition dictionary can override this setting per matrix; S2 uses it only when partition_s2 specifies it. Only partition_s2 accepts dechirp (default True), which removes and restores the scalar detector vacuum beam phase during interpolation. scan_chunk : int or None, default 8192 Process at most this many masked scan positions at once in the per-atom contraction. Bounds the scan-dependent intermediate memory so the scan can be sampled arbitrarily finely without OOM (results are independent of the value; None processes all positions in one block). contract : {“columns”, “probe”}, default “columns” How the per-atom contraction is associated (same result, different cost):
* ``"columns"`` forms the ``(n_det, B)`` intermediate
  ``SHn0 = S2c·(H·S1c)`` once per atom and applies the scan coefficients
  last (``amp = SHn0·c``). This intermediate is *scan-independent*, so the
  per-scan cost is a cheap GEMM -- best when ``P`` is very large or the crop
  window is the full grid.
* ``"probe"`` does the beam sum first, rebuilding the physical probe on the
  crop window (``probe = c·S1c``) and contracting it against the detector
  columns (``amp = S2c·(H·probe)``). This avoids the ``O(n_det·B·|Ω|)``
  intermediate and is markedly faster (~3-4x) when the crop window is small
  and ``P`` is modest -- the typical map regime. Equivalent to
  ``"columns"`` up to floating-point rounding (the contraction is reassociated).

title: API reference
text:
Returns
Tensor or (Tensor, Tensor) With qeels_axis=None: the STEM-EELS image, (P,) or scan_shape. Otherwise: (spectrum, q_pixels) where spectrum has a trailing momentum axis ((P, n_q) or scan_shape + (n_q,)) and q_pixels is the (n_q,) sorted signed-pixel frequency of each bin (physical q = q_pixels / gridsize[qeels_axis]). For "both", q_pixels has shape (n_q, 2) in (qy, qx) order, with one signed coordinate pair per retained beam; divide each column by its corresponding grid size to obtain inverse Angstroms.

ScatteringMatrix
Plane-wave scattering matrix :math:\mathcal S advanced by multislice.
Each row is the multislice-propagated plane wave for one beam in the probe-forming aperture. Advancing the matrix to a given depth and forming a probe by linear combination reproduces the elastic wave at that depth for any scan position.


PartitionedScatteringMatrix
Partitioned-PRISM scattering matrix (Pelz 2021) for STEM-EELS.
Instead of one multislice-propagated plane wave per aperture pixel, the matrix is built on a small set of Bp parent beams (a hex-ring subsample of the aperture). The probe at a scan position is synthesised by natural- neighbor interpolation of the de-tilted parent columns:
psi(r, R) = sum_p S_dt[p](r) * basis_p(r - R),
S_dt[p](r)   = S[p](r) * exp(-2 pi i g_p . r / N),      (de-tilted column)
basis_p(rho) = sum_b coeffs[b] w[b,p] exp(2 pi i g_b . rho / N),
where w[b,p] are the natural-neighbor weights expressing aperture beam b in terms of the parents. In the full-parent limit (every beam its own parent, w the identity) this is algebraically the exact per-pixel probe, so :class:ScatteringMatrix is the Bp -> B limit and serves as the oracle. Presents the advance_to / probe_at_current_plane interface of :class:ScatteringMatrix plus :meth:coeffs_at / :meth:reconstruct_columns, so it can drive either the hybrid path or the dual-scattering-matrix exit (the reconstructed columns are scalar-combinable). Accepts interpolation_factor so PRISM beam subsampling composes with partitioning. Accuracy is regime-dependent (the natural-neighbor reconstruction error).


DetectorExitSMatrix
S2: columns are detector-output beams back-propagated to the current slice.
S2_d(r) is the adjoint (transpose) multislice of the conjugate detector plane wave e_d* from the exit surface back to the current slice, so that for any wave w at that slice sum_r S2_d(r) w(r) == fft(forward_exit(w))[d] – the amplitude reaching detector beam d. Built once covering all slices (slice 0 -> exit) and :meth:peel_to advances the start slice forward (removing front slices) so it is reused across every atom.
With partition the transpose multislice is built on only Bp parent detector beams (a hex-ring subsample); the full detector columns are NNW-reconstructed on a crop window via :meth:columns_window. By reciprocity the de-tilted back-propagated columns are locally similar, so the same partitioned-PRISM interpolation applies – shrinking the resident S2 from ndet to Bp columns.

make_potential
make_potential(structure, pixels, subslices=[1.0], tiling=(1, 1), displacements=True, fractional_occupancy=True, sinc_deconvolution=True, bandwidthlimit=0.2, fe=None, device=None, dtype=torch.float32, seed=None, weights=None, weight_power=1, *, cache_fe: 'bool' = True) -> 'torch.Tensor'
Projected electrostatic potential of a structure on a pixel grid.
Evaluates, for each depth slice s and grid node n,
.. math::
V_s(\mathbf r_n) \;=\; \frac{1}{L_y L_x} \sum_{\mathbf k} M(\mathbf k)
    \Big[\sum_{Z} f_e^{Z}(\mathbf g_{\mathbf k})\,
         \tilde S_{Z,s}(\mathbf k)\Big]\,
    e^{+2\pi i (k_y n_y/N_y + k_x n_x/N_x)},
where :math:\tilde S_{Z,s} is the sinc-deconvolved DFT of the bilinear splat of the species-Z atoms assigned to slice s, :math:f_e^Z is the electron scattering factor in V Å³, :math:M is the soft band-limit mask, :math:\mathbf g_{\mathbf k} = (k_y/L_y, k_x/L_x) in Å⁻¹, and :math:L_i are the tiled supercell edges. Equivalently, and this is what it is for: the convolution of the slice’s atomic delta comb with the per-species projected atomic potential. See the module docstring for the physics and the references.

title: API reference
text:
Parameters
structure : Structure Must expose unitcell — the length-3 orthorhombic edge vector in Å — and atoms, an (natoms, 6) float array whose columns are [x, y, z, Z, occupancy, <u^2>]: x, y, z fractional coordinates nominally in [0, 1), Z the atomic number, occupancy in (0, 1], and <u^2> the one-dimensional mean-square thermal displacement in Å² (not the Debye-Waller B; B = 8 pi^2 <u^2>). Also fractional_occupancy, a bool. pixels : (2,) sequence of int Grid (Ny, Nx) covering the tiled supercell. A bare int is not accepted. subslices : float or (nss,) array_like, optional Upper fractional depths of the slices along c, non-decreasing, ending at 1.0. A bare float is treated as a single slice. title: API reference
text:
Notes
Element order is an external contract. Species are enumerated as list(set(...)) over the int32 atomic numbers, i.e. CPython’s small-int hash order, which is not sorted: {8, 42, 16, 1, 92} enumerates as [1, 8, 42, 16, 92]. Callers that precompute fe build it against that order; replacing it with sorted() would silently permute form factors between species.
Integral invariant. sum(V) * dy * dx equals sum_m occ_m * w_m**p * fe_{Z_m}(0) over all atoms including tile replicas. This is the cheapest end-to-end check of the normalisation, and the gradient with respect to w_m is correspondingly fe_{Z_m}(0)/(dy*dx).
Differentiability. Gradients flow through weights only; positions and the slice/element index maps are non-differentiable buffers.
Determinism. On CUDA, scatter-add into a float buffer accumulates in nondeterministic order, so two identical calls can differ at the ULP level even with displacements=False.

make_transmission_functions
make_transmission_functions(structure, pixels, eV, subslices: 'Sequence[float]' = (1.0,), tiling: 'Sequence[int]' = (1, 1), fe: 'Optional[Tensor]' = None, displacements: 'bool' = True, fftout: 'bool' = False, dtype: 'Optional[torch.dtype]' = None, device: 'Optional[Union[str, torch.device]]' = None, fractional_occupancy: 'bool' = True, seed: 'Optional[int]' = None, bandwidth_limit: 'Optional[Union[float, Sequence[float]]]' = 0.6666666666666666, V_abs: 'Optional[Tensor]' = None, dz: 'Optional[float]' = None, weights: 'Optional[Tensor]' = None) -> 'Tensor'
Build the band-limited multislice transmission functions of a structure.
Three stages:

Potential. Delegate to :func:scatterem.simulation.potentials.make_potential for the real projected electrostatic potential V of shape (nsubslices, Ny, Nx) in VA. (That builder applies its own, separate soft antialias filter to the potential; bandwidth_limit here is the later, harder aperture applied to the transmission function*, and is not forwarded.)
Complex exponential. Pure-elastic path,
.. math:: T_j() = (i,,V_j()),
so :math:|T| = 1 exactly. With V_abs supplied, the optical potential picks up an imaginary part :math:V^{\text{tot}} = V^{\text{DW}} + i\,\Delta z\,V^{\text{abs}} and
.. math::
T_j(\mathbf{r}) = e^{\,i\sigma V_j(\mathbf{r})}\,
                   e^{-\sigma\,\Delta z\,V^{\text{abs}}_j(\mathbf{r})},
a pure phase times a real attenuation: the Debye–Waller absorptive channel. Pass Debye–Waller-damped scattering factors through fe to make the elastic V the DW-smeared :math:V^{\text{DW}}; the absorptive sink itself arrives ready-made in V_abs.
Band limit and output space. Forward-FFT over the last two axes, zero everything outside the antialias ellipse, and either return that (fftout=True) or transform back (fftout=False, the default). In one line, for fftout=False::
T = IFFT2( M * FFT2( exp(i*sigma*V - sigma*dz*V_abs) ) )

Notes
The forward transform is unnormalised (norm="backward") and the inverse carries the full 1/(Ny*Nx), so Parseval reads sum_r |T|^2 = (1/(Ny*Nx)) * sum_q |T_hat|^2 and the DC element equals sum_r T(r). Do not switch to norm="ortho"; it would rescale the fftout=True return by sqrt(Ny*Nx).
|T| = 1 holds only on the elastic path and only before the band limit. After band-limiting it departs from unity by of order 1% for a realistic potential, and with V_abs it is strictly below 1 by construction. A vacuum (atom-free) tile gives T = 1 everywhere before the aperture, but the aperture turns that into the inverse transform of a masked delta – a sinc-like kernel with DC = 1, not the constant 1. electron_wavelength(accelerating_voltage: 'float') -> 'float'
Return the relativistic electron wavelength in Angstrom.
An electron accelerated through V volts gains kinetic energy eV. Its momentum follows from the relativistic energy-momentum relation, and the de Broglie relation turns that into a wavelength::
lambda = h / sqrt(2 m0 e V (1 + e V / (2 m0 c^2)))
The bracketed factor is the relativistic correction; it is negligible below a few hundred volts and reaches ~1.2 at 200 kV, where ignoring it would overstate the wavelength by roughly 10%.

Radial average of a corner-origin 2D array, over FFT frequency bins.
Written from the definition.
Each pixel contributes to the two bins its |q| falls between, in proportion to how close it lies to each — a linear (area-weighted) partition rather than nearest-bin assignment, which is what keeps a radial profile from developing sawtooth ripple at small radii where few pixels land per bin. The two contributions are accumulated in one pass by concatenating them, so the normalising count and the weighted sum each need a single bincount.
Args: image: 2D array with the zero frequency at [0, 0], as torch.fft produces. numpy array or torch tensor. sampling: real-space pixel size (dy, dx); the returned frequencies are in the reciprocal of that unit.
Returns: (q_bins, profile), truncated to the largest frequency represented on both axes so the tail is not built from corner pixels alone.
One deliberate difference from the replaced function: it truncated at the x axis maximum only, so with anisotropic sampling it returned bins past the shorter axis’ Nyquist, where a “ring” is really a pair of corner wedges. This truncates at the smaller of the two. On a square grid with equal sampling — every case the published figures use — the two agree to machine precision (measured max abs difference 2e-15, same bin count); with anisotropic sampling this returns a shorter profile, which matters to a caller slicing the result by index.

title: Calibration
text: Most reconstruction problems are calibration problems. The fusion weights are functions of spatial frequency, so if the mapping from detector pixels to reciprocal space is wrong, the weights are wrong, and the result is a plausible image that is quietly incorrect. This page is the short list of things to get right.

title: Calibration
text:
The reciprocal pixel size, dk
dk is measured, not assumed. The bright-field disk has a known angular radius — the convergence semi-angle you supplied — so fitting its radius in pixels gives the conversion directly:
\[ dk = \frac{\alpha}{r_{\mathrm{BF}}\,\lambda} \]
with \(r_\mathrm{BF}\) the fitted radius in pixels and \(\lambda\) the relativistic electron wavelength. Dataset4dstem.from_array runs this fit during construction, and the named datasets arrive already calibrated.
The fit sweeps a set of intensity thresholds and takes the median radius, which is what makes it insensitive to where exactly you consider the disk edge to be. It refuses rather than guesses when the pattern has no compact bright region — a fit whose radius exceeds 40% of the detector usually means the input was not an averaged diffraction pattern at all.
dk = dataset.calibrate_reciprocal_from_bright_field()
print(dataset.sampling)   # (dy, dx, dky, dkx)






Counting detectors: pass a hot-pixel threshold



On an event-counting detector a single stuck pixel can dominate the maximum the threshold sweep is relative to, and the fit then locks onto that one pixel. If your detector counts, pass hot_pixel_threshold and check the fitted radius is physically sensible before trusting it.

title: Calibration
text:
The scan rotation
The angle between the scan axes and the detector axes has to be right, and nothing downstream can infer it: the autofocus holds rotation fixed while it fits aberrations. A wrong rotation shows up as a reconstruction that is sharp along one direction and smeared along the other, or as a fused image with directional artefacts that no amount of aberration fitting removes.
If you know it from the microscope, set it:
dataset.meta.rotation = 84.0   # degrees
If you do not, the centre-of-mass field of the bright-field disk determines it: the correct rotation is the one that makes that field a gradient — curl-free — because it is the gradient of the projected potential.

title: Calibration
text:
Detector orientation
Worth checking early, because it is easy to miss and it produces a specific, recognisable failure. If the detector’s axes are flipped relative to the scan, the parallax shifts come out with the wrong handedness, defocus fits toward zero, and the aberration fit reports a suspiciously small C10 regardless of the real defocus. A defocus that will not move off zero is worth suspecting a flip rather than a fitting problem.

title: Calibration
text:
The aberration starting guess
The autofocus is a local optimisation. It needs a starting defocus, and it raises if meta.aberrations is all zero rather than descending from nothing:
dataset.meta.aberrations.array[0] = -50.0   # C10, Angstrom; defocus == -C10
dataset.determine_aberrations_(correct_order=2)
The sign matters more than the magnitude — an estimate within a factor of two is plenty, but the wrong sign can settle into a mirror-image solution with inverted contrast. Through-focus contrast inversion in direct ptychography is physical, not a bug, so a reconstruction that looks inverted may simply be on the other side of focus.

title: Calibration
text:
Scan step and upsampling
scan_step is the pitch of the scan, in Ångström. The reconstruction is upsampled relative to it, by default to the factor that brings the output pitch to what the data can support (upsample="nyquist").
That upsampling is why a scale bar needs the reconstruction’s sampling, not the dataset’s:
from scatterem.vis.reconstruction_sampling import reconstruction_sampling

sampling = reconstruction_sampling(dataset, fused)
Getting this wrong overstates the bar by the upsample factor — four-fold on the paper’s Fig. 4, which is the difference between a correct figure and a wrong one.

title: Calibration
text:
Sanity checks worth running

dk is not the placeholder. If dataset.sampling[2] is exactly 1.0, the bright-field fit fell back and everything downstream is in detector pixels, not inverse Ångström.
The reconstruction is finite. A NaN anywhere usually means a division by a zero SSNR, which in turn means an empty channel.
The bright-field radius is plausible. Print it. A radius near the detector half-width, or a couple of pixels, both mean the fit found the wrong thing.
Both channels look sensible on their own before you read the fused result. Fusion cannot rescue a channel that failed; it will just weight it down and leave a band with nothing in it.

title: Reproduce the paper
section: Numerical differences from the published figures
text:
Numerical differences from the published figures
Two are worth knowing about.
The bright-field disk fit is an independent implementation, and end to end through the crop-and-refit it lands within 0.152% of the original dk. That shifts the reciprocal scale by well under the uncertainty on the convergence angle itself, but it is not bit-identical.
Scale-bar lengths are chosen on a 1-2-5 ladder, so a bar may be a different round number than in the paper — 10 Å where the paper shows 5 Å on the same field, for instance. The bar is correct; only which round number it picks differs.

title: The method
text:
A converged probe illuminates a specimen and a pixelated detector records the full diffraction pattern at every scan position. What reaches the detector splits naturally in two, and the split is where the method starts.
Inside the bright-field disk, the transmitted beam interferes with itself. Weak-phase scattering shifts the intensity distribution across the disk in proportion to the local phase gradient, which is what single-side-band ptychography reads. That works beautifully at low and mid spatial frequencies — each frequency is measured by a pair of overlapping beams, and the overlap is large — but the overlap shrinks as the spatial frequency approaches twice the convergence angle, and past it there is none. Transfer falls to zero.
Outside the disk, scattering is incoherent to good approximation, and a dark-field detector segment sees an image that shifts with defocus and with the segment’s angle — a parallax. Correcting those shifts and summing recovers high spatial frequencies well. But a dark-field segment carries almost no low-frequency information: at low frequency the parallax shift is small and the signal is dominated by thickness and composition rather than phase.
So each channel is strong exactly where the other is weak. Neither spans the band.

title: The method
The method
text:
Sub-pixel accumulation
Tilt-corrected dark field shifts each azimuthal segment by its parallax shift and accumulates. How that shift is applied matters at low dose, and there are two options.
shift_method="fourier" zero-pads and applies a phase ramp. It is exact for dense, band-limited signals.
shift_method="drizzle" (the default) treats each input pixel as a small square drop, places it at the shifted position, and distributes its flux to the output pixels it overlaps by area — the drizzle of Fruchter & Hook (2002), specialised to pure translations on a regular grid. Because every weight is non-negative, the result is non-negative for non-negative input, and flux is conserved exactly.
The difference shows up when the frames are sparse. At very low dose a segment image is a handful of single electron counts, and Fourier shifting turns each isolated count into a sinc: roughly 20% negative side-lobes, with energy spread across the whole frame. Drizzle has no ringing to spread.






Note



The paper’s figures were produced with the Fourier path; drizzle came afterwards. Both are available, and on dense high-dose data they agree closely — on amorphous carbon the fused images correlate to 0.9992.

title: The method
text:
What this is not
The direct ptychography here is non-iterative. It is a single linear inversion of the bright-field intensity, not a phase-retrieval loop, so it has no convergence behaviour, no step size and no initialisation beyond the aberration estimate. That is why it runs in under a second on a 96² scan. It also means it inherits the weak- phase approximation: strong scatterers and thick specimens depart from it, and an iterative multislice reconstruction will do better there.
